extracted.intended_audience: DHS adjudicators and rulewriters; immigration attorneys, policy analysts, state/local agencies, advocacy groups, and other stakeholders affected by public charge rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble and regulatory text guidance describing how DHS will determine whether a noncitizen is "likely at any time to become a public charge," which benefits are considered, statutory factors to be weighed, exclusions, procedural requirements (forms, bonds), and required analyses for regulatory review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family Policymaking Assessment — section 654 factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1999 requires agencies to assess whether a regulatory action affects family well-being by evaluating seven items: (1) strengthens or erodes family stability or safety and marital commitment; (2) strengthens or erodes parental authority/rights in education, nurture, supervision of children; (3) helps the family perform its functions or substitutes governmental activity for the function; (4) increases or decreases disposable income or poverty of families and children; (5) whether proposed benefits justify the financial impact on the family; (6) whether the action may be carried out by State/local government or by the family; (7) whether the action establishes a policy concerning youth behavior and societal norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS must determine whether a Family Policymaking Assessment is required and, if so, evaluate positive and negative impacts on family well-being. DHS explains how the rule may reduce chilling effects and thereby indirectly support children and families' access to health care, nutrition, and housing assistance; DHS concluded this rule would not have a deleterious effect on family well-being relative to the No Action Baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Orders 12866 and 13563: cost-benefit and values considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: E.O. 12866 and E.O. 13563 direct agencies to assess costs and benefits of regulatory alternatives and, when permitted, proceed only if benefits justify costs; select approaches that maximize net benefits; and, to the extent appropriate and consistent with law, give consideration to values difficult to quantify, including equity, human dignity, fairness, and distributive impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory planning and review must quantify costs and benefits where possible, but also explicitly consider equity and distributive impacts alongside quantified metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-4: treatment of transfer payments
rubrics_metrics.description: As OMB Circular A-4 prescribes, changes in transfer payments are neither costs nor benefits of the rule and are treated separately in the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated reductions in federal or state transfer payments (e.g., due to chilling effects) should not be counted as costs or benefits in the benefit-cost calculation but should be discussed separately and in the regulatory accounting statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of public benefits considered
rubrics_metrics.description: This rule limits consideration to "public cash assistance for income maintenance" and "long-term institutionalization at government expense." Public cash assistance for income maintenance includes cash assistance provided under TANF, SSI, and general assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS clarifies that nearly all other benefits (e.g., SNAP and other nutrition programs, CHIP, Medicaid except for long-term institutionalization, housing benefits, immunizations/testing for communicable diseases, and other supplemental or special-purpose benefits) are not considered in public charge inadmissibility determinations. DHS also clarified it will not consider receipt of, certification, or approval for future receipt of public benefits not referenced in 8 CFR 212.21(b) or (c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from consideration of public benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider: (1) any public benefits received during periods when the noncitizen was present in an immigration category exempt from the public charge ground; (2) any public benefits received by noncitizens eligible for resettlement assistance, entitlement programs, and other benefits available to refugees admitted under INA section 207; and (3) applying for a public benefit on one's own behalf or on behalf of another does not constitute receipt unless the noncitizen is also a named recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exclusions are codified to avoid considering benefits received during exempt statuses or refugee-type assistance, and to ensure that assistance provided to others (or assisting with applications) is not treated as the applicant's receipt of benefits unless they are a beneficiary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors and totality of the circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers will consider, as part of a totality of the circumstances, statutory minimum factors: the noncitizen's age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills, and the Affidavit of Support under section 213A where required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS uses a totality-of-the-circumstances framework. The preamble notes changes to how each factor will be assessed and that Form I-485 collects information relevant to these factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written denial must include discussion of each statutory factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule maintains the language from the 1999 Interim Field Guidance that every written denial decision issued by USCIS based on the public charge ground of inadmissibility must include a discussion of each of the statutory factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators must document how each statutory factor was considered in any written denial, ensuring reasoned explanations addressing each factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of past or current receipt of cash assistance and long-term institutionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will continue to consider past and current receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization at government expense because these may be indicative of primary dependence on the government for subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such receipt is weighed in the totality of circumstances taking into account amount, duration, and recency. DHS emphasizes that past or current receipt alone is not a sufficient basis to determine likelihood of becoming a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of disability and institutionalization evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule clarifies that disability will never alone form the basis for determining that a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge. DHS will accept evidence that institutionalization violates the individual's rights under disability laws, including the ADA and section 504.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes that some institutionalization may occur due to lack of alternative services (e.g., HCBS unavailability). Accepting such evidence may affect consideration of long-term institutionalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health factor: use of Form I-693
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's health using the Report of Medical Examination and Vaccination record (Form I-693).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Form I-693 is already required for I-485 filers, using it reduces additional information collection burdens and provides clarity on what constitutes evidence for the health factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family status metric: household size
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's family status using household size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule adds a definition of household to be used in connection with family status and assets/resources/financial status factors; this informs how household composition affects assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assets, resources, and financial status: household income/assets/liabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider the noncitizen's assets, resources, and financial status using the household's income, assets, and liabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude any income from public benefits listed in 8 CFR 212.21(b) and income or assets from illegal activities (e.g., proceeds from illegal gambling or drug sales). Adjudicators should evaluate the household's financial picture rather than only the applicant's individual finances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills: degrees, certifications, licenses, and work-acquired skills
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will consider education and skills using degrees, certifications, licenses, skills obtained through work experience or educational programs, and educational certificates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This evidence is used to assess self-sufficiency potential and labor market prospects in the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bright-line rule against considering benefits received by applicant's dependents
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule states a bright-line rule against considering the receipt of public benefits by an applicant's dependents (such as a U.S. citizen child in a mixed-status household).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits received by family members (dependents) should not be attributed to the noncitizen applicant in public charge determinations, reducing confusion for mixed-status households.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying for benefits on behalf of another not treated as receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying for public benefits on behalf of another person (or the receipt of public benefits solely on behalf of another) does not constitute receipt of public benefits by the noncitizen, unless the noncitizen is also a named recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that assistance in application or facilitating benefits for others is not treated as the applicant's own benefit receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond authority and bond process
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule adds a provision permitting officers, in their discretion, to consider offering public charge bonds to adjustment of status applicants inadmissible only under INA section 212(a)(4), and includes provisions for bond cancellation and breach determination and designated forms (including Form I-356).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions are intended to make public charge bonds operationally feasible for adjustment of status cases; DHS expects minimal use and estimates nominal form-filing costs for applicants if used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form I-485 information collection standards and burden minimization
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS revised Form I-485 information collection to streamline questions (changing open-ended narrative-style questions to multiple-choice) and reduced the estimated time burden increase for the revised Form I-485 from 1.5 hours to 0.75 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms should collect information relevant to statutory factors while minimizing familiarization and administrative costs; revisions aim to reduce applicant time burden and downstream administrative inquiries to benefits-granting agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory analysis baselines and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS compares impacts relative to two baselines: the No Action Baseline (1999 Interim Field Guidance) and the Pre-Guidance Baseline (trajectory before issuance of the 1999 Interim Field Guidance). The alternative analysis relates to an alternative consistent with the 2019 Final Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory analysis should present quantified and non-quantified costs and benefits relative to these baselines, provide multi-year net cost estimates (including discounted totals at standard discount rates), and present accounting statements as required by OMB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of chilling effects and downstream societal impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS must consider potential chilling effects of policies governing public charge determinations — including evidence that the 2019 Final Rule caused fear, confusion, and reduced enrollment in benefits among eligible persons — and the downstream impacts (worse health outcomes, increased ER use, communicable disease prevalence, uncompensated care, poverty, housing instability, reduced productivity and educational attainment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory decisions and analyses should assess chilling effects, weigh them in context of statutory interpretation and administrative goals, and aim to minimize undue confusion; impacts on State/local economies and businesses should be discussed even if transfer payments are not counted as costs/benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of primary dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule clarifies that 'primary dependence' connotes significant reliance on the government for support and means something more than dependence that is merely transient or supplementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators should interpret 'primary dependence' as substantial, sustained reliance and not label transient or supplemental assistance as indicative of likely future primary dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarification that the rule does not determine benefit eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the statutory public charge ground of inadmissibility nor this final rule governs eligibility for public benefits; the rule does not address which noncitizens are or should be eligible to receive public benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will make clear in this rule and communications who is and is not subject to the public charge ground of inadmissibility; adjudicators and benefit agencies should not conflate public_charge consideration with benefit eligibility determinations.
